opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few big ones, and honestly I'm uncertain about a lot of this.

The first is just whether the tasks we measure on keep tracking what we actually care about. A lot of our work, like the time-horizon measurements, uses tasks that are fairly well-specified, self-contained, and automatically scorable. That's partly by necessity: you need something you can run hundreds of times and grade reliably. But real-world work, and especially the work that matters most for risk, like doing AI research autonomously, is messier. It involves ambiguous goals, long feedback loops, coordinating with other people, and deciding what to work on in the first place. So an open question is how much performance on our clean tasks transfers to those messier settings. We've done some work looking at "messiness" factors and whether models do worse on messier tasks, and there's some signal there, but I don't think we've nailed it.

Related to that is extrapolation. If you see a trend, like the length of tasks models can complete doubling every several months, it's tempting to draw the line forward and say "by this date, models can do month-long projects." But it's unclear whether that trend holds, whether it speeds up because AI starts accelerating AI research, or whether it hits some wall where the remaining skills are qualitatively different. The trend is useful evidence, but I'd be cautious about treating it as a law.

Then there's the elicitation question. When we evaluate a model, we're trying to measure what it can do, not just what it does with whatever scaffold we threw together. Developers and users keep finding better ways to get capabilities out of models, with better agent scaffolds, more inference compute, and tool use. So any measurement is something like a lower bound, and how loose that bound is matters a lot for risk estimates. And as models get more situationally aware, there's a further worry that they might behave differently when they recognize they're being evaluated, which would undermine the whole approach in a more fundamental way.

There's also a benchmark saturation and construction problem. Building tasks that take skilled humans many hours or days, and that we can still score reliably, is really expensive. Measuring the frontier gets harder as the frontier moves, and getting good human baselines for those long tasks is its own challenge.

And finally, there's the gap between capabilities and risk itself. Capability evals tell you something like "this model could plausibly do X." Turning that into "here's how risky it is" requires a bunch of other assumptions: about deployment, about whether anyone would actually try to misuse it, about the model's propensities, and about what safeguards exist. As capabilities get higher, I think capability evals alone become less sufficient. At some point the answer is just "yes, it can do the dangerous thing," and then what matters is alignment, control, and monitoring, which are harder to measure. So figuring out how capability evaluations fit into a broader safety case, rather than standing on their own, is probably one of the most important open questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether clean-task performance transfers to autonomous AI research and says high capabilities make capability evaluations less sufficient, but it does not ask how to estimate risk once systems can perform AI research very effectively.

r002.rationale: The response says risk estimates depend on deployment, misuse, propensities, and safeguards, but it does not connect those factors to rejecting the claim that highly effective AI research necessarily makes risk maximal.

r003.rationale: The response mentions monitoring as difficult to measure, but does not propose developing metrics of AI monitorability as a direction for METR’s evaluation work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few that I find myself worrying about a lot.

The first is just how long our evaluations keep working. A lot of what METR does is give models tasks that we think are proxies for dangerous or economically important capabilities, and then measure how far along they are. The time horizon work is the clearest example: we look at the length of a task a human expert would take, and ask whether models can reliably do it. That's been a really useful framing, but it has an expiration date. If models get to the point where they're doing tasks that take humans weeks or months, it becomes extremely expensive to construct those tasks, to get human baselines, and to grade them. So one open question is basically, what does an evaluation even look like when the thing you're measuring is harder than what a small team can realistically construct and check?

The second is about the gap between what we measure in a sandbox and what actually happens in the world. Our tasks tend to be fairly clean. They have a specification, they have a scoring function, they're self-contained. Real work isn't like that. It's messy, it involves figuring out what the task even is, coordinating with people, dealing with ambiguous feedback. We've seen cases where models look great on benchmarks and then developers using them in practice report that they're much less helpful than the numbers would suggest. So there's a real question of how much our capability numbers tell you about risk, which ultimately is a question about what happens when these systems are deployed into a real environment rather than a test harness. I don't think we have a great answer yet, and it cuts both ways. Models could be more dangerous than our evals suggest because they're better in the wild on some axis we don't capture, or less dangerous because the benchmark overstates them.

Third, there's the problem of models knowing they're being evaluated. We've already seen hints of this: models noticing that a task looks like a test, commenting on it in their reasoning. Right now I don't think that's a huge distorting factor, but if you imagine a world where models could behave differently when they think they're being watched, then a capability eval is only measuring the floor of what the model can do, not the ceiling. And that's exactly the wrong thing for risk estimation. For risk you care about the ceiling. So a big open question is whether we can design evaluations that remain informative even if the model is sophisticated about the fact that it's being measured, or whether we need completely different techniques for that, more interpretability-based or more about the training process than about behavior.

The fourth thing I think about is the connection between capability and risk, which people often treat as kind of obvious and it really isn't. Our evals tell you something like, this model can autonomously do a two-hour software task with some reliability. Translating that into a probability of some bad outcome requires a bunch of other assumptions: about what the model would be motivated to do, about how it would be deployed, about what safeguards are in place. Capability is necessary for a lot of the risks we care about, but it's nowhere near sufficient. So I think there's a real question of whether capability evals should be seen as one input into a much larger risk model, and then who builds that larger model and how we validate it. Right now I think the honest answer is that we're mostly producing the capability input, and the rest is done fairly informally.

And then there's a more sociological question, which is whether any of this actually affects decisions. An evaluation is only useful for estimating risk if someone acts on the estimate. We've been in a decent position where labs let us test models before release and seem to take the results seriously, but that's based on voluntary arrangements. If the competitive pressure gets stronger, or if the results get inconvenient, there's no guarantee that continues. So part of the future usefulness question isn't technical at all, it's about whether the institutional setup survives contact with much more capable and much more commercially valuable models.

I'd say I'm fairly optimistic about the next couple of years. The methods we have are telling us real things, the trends are legible, and people are paying attention. Beyond that, I think the honest position is that we're going to have to keep reinventing what evaluation means, probably more than once.

astra-6.text:
I think a big open question is how well performance on the tasks we can evaluate translates into the ability to do consequential things in the world. You can measure whether a model completes a particular software engineering task, but there are additional steps between that and saying it could autonomously carry out a dangerous project. It might need to operate for much longer, recover from mistakes, or deal with situations that aren’t very well specified.

There’s also the question of how much the evaluations depend on the way we elicit capabilities. If a model fails with the tools and prompting we give it, would it succeed with a better scaffold, more inference compute, or some additional training? That makes it difficult to interpret a negative result as evidence that the capability is absent.

And then, even if we could measure capabilities really well, how much would that tell us about risk? Risk also depends on how systems are deployed, what access they have, and whether people can reliably supervise them. So I think these evaluations can be a useful input, but an important open question is how to connect their results to specific threat models—and how much warning they’ll give us before the capabilities in those threat models actually emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one big question is how well performance on the tasks we can evaluate translates into the ability to do consequential things in the real world. We can measure whether a model completes a particular task under particular conditions, but there’s still a gap between that and saying how much risk the model poses.

And part of that gap is about elicitation. If a model fails, is that because it lacks the capability, or because we haven’t found the right scaffolding, tools, or prompting? How much better would it do if someone invested substantially more effort? That matters a lot if we want a negative evaluation result to provide reassurance.

There’s also a question about how representative our tasks will remain as models get more capable. We need tasks that are tractable to evaluate, but the things we ultimately care about can involve long time horizons, messy environments, and interactions with people. It’s an open question how reliably we can extrapolate from one to the other.

So I’d distinguish measuring capabilities from estimating risk. I think these evaluations can give us useful evidence about capabilities. How much confidence that evidence should give us about risk—and especially about the absence of risk—is a harder question.

r002.rationale: It says capability evidence does not directly determine risk, but does not address or reject the claim that strong AI research ability necessarily makes risk maximal.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify developing metrics of AI monitorability as a direction for METR’s evaluations.
